item.title: What happens if air traffic control goes down? A look inside the system after the FAA ground stop
item.description:
Last Friday the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after an outage in air traffic control's telecommunications system — a timely reminder of how much of holiday flying depends on a system most travelers never think about. The FAA's Air Traffic Organization coordinates roughly 44,000 flights a day across 29 million square miles of airspace, with about 5,500 planes aloft at peak times.

Control works as a relay rather than a single handoff: one national command center oversees 21 zones, each with its own control center, which pass flights down to regional TRACON facilities and finally to airport towers. If a pilot loses radio contact, they squawk 7600 and fly their last approved plan while controllers route everyone else around them. The November 13 outage reportedly traced back to newly installed hardware at a radio transmitter site that overloaded the system across 17 airspace zones, prompting the FAA to pause departures and guide some 3,500 planes already airborne safely to their destinations.

Sources

  • The Pour Over: What Happens if Air Traffic Control Goes Down?

item.title: ICJ finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against the Rohingya
item.description:
The United Nations' International Court of Justice has found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority, marking the Southeast Asian nation as the first state violator of the 1948 Genocide Convention. The court ruled 9-6 on Thursday that Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a major part of the Rohingya population, destroyed evidence of crimes, and failed to prosecute perpetrators.

The Rohingya, a majority-Muslim group, faced decades of discrimination in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar. In August 2017, after attacks on more than 30 police posts, Myanmar's forces and Buddhist mobs responded with a campaign that killed around 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to refugee camps in Bangladesh — now the largest in the world. Myanmar maintains its operations were counterterrorism. Next steps are unclear, as the ICJ lacks enforcement powers.

Sources

  • The Pour Over: Rohingya Genocide

item.title: Top officials face questions on a week of outages — and a rising threat from Iran
item.description:
Top Trump officials went to Capitol Hill Wednesday for their annual question-and-answer session on national security threats, and the topic on everyone's mind was outages. Homeland Security Secretary Mullin, FBI Deputy Director Raia, and National Intelligence Director Clayton acknowledged the suspicious timing of the FAA, Microsoft, Apple, Chase, and NSA outages while reiterating that they weren't a coordinated attack.

Officials did flag one coordinated threat: Iran. Director Clayton warned that threats have "substantially increased" at home and abroad, declining to comment on reports of a "dirty bomb" in Washington. The need for reassurance comes as some Americans are panic-buying toilet paper and generators — a sign that, whatever the official line, public confidence is fraying.

item.title: Trump, Putin, and Xi hold their first three-way talks and adopt a 'Declaration toward Peace'
item.description:
Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping held their first-ever face-to-face-to-face talks yesterday. The three leaders adopted a "Declaration toward Peace," affirming that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." They also agreed to reform the United Nations in their roles as permanent members of the Security Council and to increase their countries' petroleum production.

A trilateral summit of the world's three most powerful leaders is historic on its own terms, though the substance — a peace declaration, UN reform, and more oil — will be judged by what follows rather than what's announced. For now, the image of the three leaders at one very large table is the story.

Sources

  • The Pour Over: Rohingya Genocide

item.title: The Pour Over: "Have You Tried Restarting It?"
item.description:
The Pour Over's November 19 edition leads with "Have You Tried Restarting It?" — a nod to the classic first line of tech support. The newsletter's daily briefing typically pairs the day's top stories with a concise, faith-informed take, and this edition's lead plays on the universal experience of fixing a glitchy device the simplest way possible.

Beyond the headline, the full text of this edition wasn't readable in the feed, so the specific stories covered today aren't captured here. The Pour Over remains the topic's only source for the day, and no other general-news items arrived.
